newsitem.title: UK: FEATURE - Four events shaped Britain's Labour leader Blair.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Four events shaped Britain's Labour leader Blair.

text.p: Watching Tony Blair on the election stump, it's hard to believe that until 1994 he was just another member of parliament to the vast majority of Britons.
Even three years ago there were few indications Blair was the man who would rip "socialism" out of Labour and give his party an odds-on chance of ending 18 years of Conservative rule.
His road to the Labour leadership, and a tilt at the top job in British politics, has had its share of triumphs and setbacks. But four events stand out as landmarks on his road to power.

The death of former Labour leader John Smith in May 1994 was probably the defining moment of Blair's life, but his reaction to the murder of two-year-old Jamie Bulger in Liverpool 15 months earlier marked him out as a politician to watch.

Bulger's body was found lying on a railway line after he was abducted by two young boys. Britons were horrified but neither church leaders nor ministers, perhaps fearful of being accused of making political capital out of the crime, addressed what it said about the state of their nation.
Blair, a father of three and a committed Christian, decided to speak out. He called the Bulger murder an "ugly manifestation of a society that is unworthy of that name.

"The news bulletins of the last week have been like hammer blows struck against the sleeping conscience of the country, urging us to wake up and look unflinchingly at what we see," Blair told party workers in central England.

He was widely applauded for his appeal from the heart. His views added meat to his well-worn catchphrase that society should be tough on crime but also on its causes such as unemployment, social deprivation and alienation.

Blair had encroached on areas of politics -- law and order, and individual responsibility -- that Conservatives considered their natural patch. It was an exercise he was to repeat frequently after he became leader in July 1994.
BLAIR SEEN BY LABOUR MEMBERS AS VOTE WINNER

Smith's death from a heart attack shook Labour to its roots but within hours Blair, who had felt Smith was not pursuing the revamping of Labour with enough vigour, was installed as favourite to succeed him.
"It was like the tiger had jumped out of the pussy cat's skin," said one senior Labour official as Blair set about convincing the party he was their man of the hour.
Blair used a mixture of charm and hard-edged realism to persuade his friend and fellow-moderniser Gordon Brown, considered by many to be Smith's natural successor, not to stand against him.

Blair's election was a foregone conclusion long before the internal voting was complete. But many voted for him because they thought he had best chance of winning power at the next election, and not because they supported his plans for Labour.

That Blair would accelerate Smith's policy of change in party policy was never in doubt. But the speed with which he undertook a total revamp of tenets held dear by traditional Labour voters was breathtaking.

Just three months after his election as leader, he took aim at the party's fundamental belief in the nationalisation of key economic sectors, the totemic Clause Four of the party's old rule book inscribed on every Labour supporter's membership card. In his speech at the 1994 party conference, Blair announced he planned to rewrite Labour's constitution for the next century. When aides confirmed that this involved scrapping Clause Four, left-wingers were appalled.
Crucially, Blair had already won the support of deputy leader John Prescott, a left-winger with strong trade union links seen as the conscience of traditional socialists.

Blair, nicknamed "Bambi" by the Conservative press for his youthful inexperience and "Blur" for his perceived lack of policy definition, staked his leadership on getting approval for rewriting Clause Four.

"Those who seriously believe we cannot improve on words written for the world of 1918 when we are now in 1995 are not learning from our history but living it," he said. At a special conference in April 1995, the new-look clause espousing competition and cooperation rather than common ownership of the means of production won 65 percent backing.
Blair's electoral popularity soared and his party rode a wave of support that now puts it 25 points ahead in opinion polls over the unpopular, stumbling Conservatives.

But, as many opponents pointed out, Blair -- a 43-year-old lawyer -- is largely untried on the wider political stage. A member of parliament since 1983, he has never held a government post or an executive post in local or trade union politics.
BLAIR INEXPERIENCED IN DEALING WITH SUDDEN CRISES
His inexperience in dealing with dissent and sudden crises was revealed starkly in January 1996 by a personal decision by Harriet Harman, Labour's social security spokeswoman.
Harman, a close Blair ally, contravened official Labour policy by choosing to send her son to a London school that selects pupils according to their academic achievement.
The decision caused uproar among Labour activists and ordinary voters fed up with falling educational standards but with no chance of avoiding poor schools.
Many accused Harman, who is deeply unpopular with the Labour left wing, of hypocrisy. But Blair stuck by his friend, warning he might resign if Harman was not backed.
Blair won the day, but has since admitted the affair was his lowest moment -- and his handling of it his biggest error -- since becoming Labour leader.
"I thought the reaction was way over the top, but I should have gone public more quickly and explained it," he said.
It raised doubts among voters about his reactions under pressure and revealed a petulance in the supposedly cool Blair when faced with rebellion.
Since the Harman affair, he and his acolytes have clamped down even harder on any sign of revolt or policy disagreement.
But the left wing has not gone away, and may be waiting for the time when Blair is in power. How he reacts then will show if he has the mettle -- and metal -- to become a great leader.
